intro: Rachmaninoff records Chopin’s Minute Waltz for Victor in 1923, bringing one composer-pianist’s hands to another’s quicksilver writing. A long melody and an unaccompanied trill interrupt the famous circling notes.

sections.label: A · Quavers around A♭
sections.mNote: The left hand waits before joining the dance

sections.label: B · The singing middle
sections.mNote: Sostenuto: longer notes above the waltz accompaniment

sections.label: A′ · The running notes return
sections.mNote: The circling figure returns, then the bass joins

sections.label: Coda · D♭ major closes the dance
sections.mNote: The final scale ends in a firm chord

cues.title: One hand starts the dance
cues.text: Only the right hand plays at first: a quick loop around A♭, marked leggiero. When the bass enters, its single low note and two answering chords make the three beats plain. The melody keeps running across them.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Victor, April 1923
cues.text: On 5 April 1923 Rachmaninoff records this waltz for Victor. The day’s sessions also include his playing of a piano arrangement of Strauss’s The Blue Danube. The composer of vast concertos is at work on music for a single record side.
cues.evidence: Discography of American Historical Recordings, sessions for 5 April 1923; Chopin matrix B-24192 and Strauss C-27732. https://adp.library.ucsb.edu/index.php/date/browse/1923-04-05

cues.title: A trill without a bass
cues.text: The accompaniment stops. A long trill occupies the right hand alone, hanging over the gap before the circling quavers resume. For a few bars, Chopin removes the waltz’s feet from the floor.
cues.evidence: Peters edition, bars 69–77: trill above a resting left hand, followed by the unaccompanied running figure. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=483

composer.born: 1 March 1810 by his family’s reckoning; the parish register gives 22 February, Żelazowa Wola, Duchy of Warsaw
composer.epithet: He brought the opera singer’s breath and the mazurka’s wayward accents to a piano that could whisper across a room.
facts: Wojciech Żywny; composition with Józef Elsner in Warsaw, 1826–29
Warsaw · Paris from 1831 · summers at Nohant
Piano lessons, publishing and occasional concerts
The piano, from a few lines of mazurka to concertos and sonatas
composer.background:
In February 1832, a twenty-one-year-old Polish pianist played in the Pleyel rooms in Paris. Chopin had arrived the previous autumn, with two concertos behind him. The concert caught the attention of the city’s publishers; teaching soon supplied his living. He would spend the rest of his life in a profession that depended on people hearing him at close quarters. The great public virtuosos travelled from triumph to triumph. Chopin stayed in Paris and gave lessons.

He was born at Żelazowa Wola in 1810. His father, Nicolas, had come from France and worked as a tutor; his mother, Justyna Krzyżanowska, was Polish. They moved to Warsaw while Fryderyk was still a baby, when Nicolas obtained a teaching post at the Lyceum. At seven the boy already had a polonaise in print. Wojciech Żywny taught him the piano, with Bach and Mozart among his models; Józef Elsner later gave him a rigorous training in composition at Warsaw’s Main School of Music.
